title: A day of patience
hookLine: a monk heading to a rough place calls the people who insult him good
tomorrow: is a kind lie ever the right thing to say?

lines: THE BUS. THE WEATHER. REPLY ALL.
HOW GOOD. THEY DIDN'T HIT ME.
cards: The everyday complaints are small: the bus, the weather, the coworker who replies all. One discourse has a monk who seems to have run out of complaints entirely, and his reason is odd.

His name is Punna, and he wants to go and live in Sunaparanta, where, the Buddha warns him, the people are fierce and rough. What if they insult you? Then, Punna says, I'll think: how good these people are.

teach.b: The Buddha presses. And if they hit you? Then I'll think, how good they are, they didn't throw stones.
And stones? They didn't use a stick. A stick?
The puzzle is why this isn't just denial. Punna isn't pretending the insult is nice. He sees it exactly, an insult, and then he sees what it isn't.
Every rough thing that comes, he sets beside something worse that didn't. That's patience as a habit of mind, and it starves complaint at the root.

teach.h: A COMPLAINT SAYS: NOT TO ME.
teach.b: A complaint says: this shouldn't be happening to me.

teach.h: NAME IT, DROP THE EXTRA LINE.
teach.b: Punna says: this is happening, it could be worse, and I can bear it. The Buddha's reply is approval. With such self-control and calm, he says, you'll be able to live there.
The discourse says Punna went, and people there took up the teaching through him.
So a day without complaints isn't a day without problems. It's a day of naming them plainly, without the extra line that says the world owes you better.

how: The Punnovada Sutta is often taught as a model of patience, and some Buddhists take up a day or a week of no complaining as a practice of khanti.

games.q: what does “a day of patience” mean?
o: a day of fasting from food and from talk
keeping every hard feeling bottled up inside
naming what's hard without adding a grumble

games.q: Punna's turn of mind — tap the pairs.
p: a monk who sees the good in rough people
at least they didn't hit me

s: a no-complaint day means pretending everything is fine
Punna sees the insult exactly; he just drops the extra grumble.
the Buddha warned Punna that the people there were rough
and approved when Punna said how he'd bear it.
Punna asked the Buddha to send someone else instead
he wanted to go, and the discourse says he went.

games.q: your flight is delayed three hours and the whole gate is groaning. what would Punna's turn of mind sound like?
o: delayed, not cancelled; there's time to eat and call home.
this always happens to me; the airline should be ashamed.
it's fine, i'm totally fine, nothing is wrong at all.
games.why: Punna names the hard thing exactly, then sees what it isn't. no denial, and no extra grumble.

practice: Get up and walk slowly for about a minute, around the room or down a hall. Each time a small complaint shows up, my feet, the cold, the noise, name it plainly and add Punna's turn: and it could be worse.
Then settle back down for the rest of the sit.

wordCard.voice: A day of patience: a day of naming what's hard plainly, without the complaint on top.

orig.note: Pali name of the monk who chose to live among rough people in Sunaparanta.

carryVoice: Here's your line: no complaints, which still leaves room for problems, just not the extra grumble. See you then.

sources.ref: MN 145, Punnovada Sutta (also SN 35.88): Punna and the people of Sunaparanta
